title: Contingency Fees Explained: Percentages, Legal Caps and Net Recovery (2026)
description: How contingency fees work: written-agreement rules, federal and state fee caps, and a worked example of costs taken before vs. after the fee.
h1: How does a contingency fee work?
summary: With a contingency fee the lawyer takes an agreed percentage of any money recovered and charges no fee if nothing is recovered, although case costs may still be owed depending on the agreement. ABA Model Rule 1.5(c) requires a written agreement signed by the client that states the percentages and whether costs are deducted before or after the fee. Some laws cap the percentage, for example 20% of an administrative settlement and 25% after suit under the Federal Tort Claims Act, and 25% or 33% in California medical malpractice cases.
body:
The basic deal

In a contingency arrangement the lawyer is paid a share of what you recover, by settlement or judgment, instead of an hourly fee. If there is no recovery, there is no fee. The lawyer usually advances the case costs, such as filing fees, records, depositions and experts, and is repaid from the recovery.

No national rule sets the percentage. It is set by your agreement, must be reasonable under ABA Model Rule 1.5(a), and in some kinds of cases is capped by statute or court rule[1]. Contingency fees are not allowed for criminal defense, or in divorce matters where the fee would depend on securing the divorce or on the amount of alimony, support or property awarded[1].

Costs before or after the fee: a worked example

The single clause that most changes what you take home is whether case costs are deducted before the percentage is applied or after. Rule 1.5(c) requires the agreement to say which[1].

Illustrative example. A claim settles for $90,000. The agreement sets a one-third fee. The lawyer advanced $6,000 in case costs, and a health insurer has a $10,000 lien on the recovery. (All figures are assumptions chosen for the arithmetic.)

Same settlement, two cost clauses
StepFee on gross (costs after fee)Fee on net (costs before fee)
Settlement$90,000$90,000
Costs deducted firstNo$90,000 − $6,000 = $84,000
Lawyer's fee (1/3)$90,000 × 1/3 = $30,000$84,000 × 1/3 = $28,000
Costs repaid to lawyer$6,000(already deducted)
Lien repaid$10,000$10,000
You receive$90,000 − $30,000 − $6,000 − $10,000 = $44,000$84,000 − $28,000 − $10,000 = $46,000

The net-first clause is worth $2,000 to the client here: one-third of the $6,000 in costs. The bigger the costs, the bigger the gap.

To test your own numbers, use the contingency fee calculator.

Percentages that change by stage

Many agreements raise the percentage if a lawsuit is filed, if the case goes to trial, or if there is an appeal. Florida's bar rules show what that looks like in a real schedule: fees above these levels are presumed excessive in covered cases, including 33⅓% of a recovery up to $1 million before the defendant answers, 40% after the answer, and an extra 5% if an appeal or post-judgment relief is needed[2]. Read the stage triggers carefully: "filing suit" and "answer filed" can happen months apart and can move the percentage.

What the written agreement must say

Under ABA Model Rule 1.5(c), a contingency agreement must be in writing and signed by the client, and it must state[1]:

  • how the fee is determined, including the percentage that applies if the case settles, goes to trial or is appealed;
  • litigation and other expenses that will be deducted from the recovery;
  • whether those expenses are deducted before or after the fee is calculated;
  • any expenses you must pay whether or not you win.

When the case ends, the lawyer must give you a written statement showing the outcome and, if there is a recovery, how the money was divided[1]. Some states add protections. In Florida, for example, the lawyer must give you a signed Statement of Client's Rights before you sign, and the contract must let you cancel within 3 business days[2].

Federal fee caps

Federal limits on contingency-style fees (checked October 2026)
Claim typeCap
Federal Tort Claims Act (claims against the U.S. government)20% of an administrative settlement; 25% of a judgment or a settlement after suit is filed[3]
Camp Lejeune Justice Act claims20% of an administrative settlement; 25% of a settlement in litigation[4]
Social Security disability (fee agreement process)Lesser of 25% of past-due benefits or $9,200[5]

Charging more than the FTCA allows is a federal offense punishable by a fine of up to $2,000, up to one year in prison, or both[3].

State caps we verified

Most state caps apply to medical malpractice or workers' compensation, not to ordinary injury claims. This list is not exhaustive; other states may have rules we have not verified.

Selected state contingency-fee limits
StateCase typeLimit
CaliforniaMedical malpractice25% if settled before suit or arbitration is filed; 33% after[6]
New YorkMedical, dental and podiatric malpractice30% of first $250,000; 25% of next $250,000; 20% of next $500,000; 15% of next $250,000; 10% above $1.25 million[7]
FloridaMedical liabilityClaimant keeps at least 70% of the first $250,000 and 90% above that, excluding costs[8]
IllinoisMedical malpractice33⅓% of all sums recovered[9]
MassachusettsMedical malpractice40% of first $150,000; 33⅓% of next $150,000; 30% of next $200,000; 25% above $500,000[10]
MaineHealth care negligence33⅓% of first $100,000; 25% of next $100,000; 20% above $200,000[11]
NevadaProfessional negligence against health care providers35% of the amount recovered[12]
UtahMedical malpractice33⅓% of the amount recovered[13]
ConnecticutPersonal injury, wrongful death, property damageSliding scale from 33⅓% of the first $300,000 down to 10% above $1.2 million[14]
MichiganPersonal injury and wrongful deathOne-third of the amount recovered[15]
IllinoisWorkers' compensation20% of compensation recovered, with exceptions after a hearing[16]
TexasWorkers' compensation25% of income benefits[17]
MinnesotaWorkers' compensation20% of the first $275,000; total fees for one injury capped at $55,000[18]

Example: how a sliding cap works. A New York medical malpractice case recovers $600,000. Under Judiciary Law § 474-a the maximum fee is 30% × $250,000 = $75,000, plus 25% × $250,000 = $62,500, plus 20% × $100,000 = $20,000, for a total of $157,500[7]. That is 26.25% of the recovery, compared with $200,000 at a flat one-third.

See the guides for medical malpractice, workers' comp and personal injury for more detail.

Questions to ask before you sign

  • What percentage applies at each stage, and what exactly triggers the next stage?
  • Are costs deducted before or after the fee?
  • Do I owe costs if we lose?
  • Is any statute or court rule capping the fee in my type of case?
  • How are medical liens and insurer reimbursement claims handled, and does the fee apply to amounts paid to lienholders?
  • What happens to the fee if I change lawyers or the lawyer withdraws?
  • Will another firm share the fee? Under Rule 1.5(e), a split between firms requires your written agreement to each lawyer's share[1].

Need a lawyer who works this way? See how to find a contingency fee lawyer.

faq.q: What percentage do contingency lawyers take?
faq.a: There is no national standard; the percentage is whatever the written agreement says, subject to the rule that fees be reasonable and to any statutory cap. Many agreements use different percentages for settlement before suit, after suit and after trial, so compare the whole schedule, not one number.

faq.q: Do I pay anything if I lose a contingency case?
faq.a: You owe no fee, but you may owe case costs if the agreement says so. The ABA model rule requires the agreement to state any expenses you must pay whether or not you win, so look for that clause.

faq.q: Is the contingency fee calculated before or after costs?
faq.a: It depends on your agreement, which must say which method applies. Calculating the fee after costs are deducted leaves more money for the client, by roughly the fee percentage multiplied by the costs.

faq.q: Can I negotiate a contingency fee?
faq.a: Yes. You can ask for a lower percentage, a lower percentage if the case settles early, or costs deducted before the fee. Lawyers do not have to agree, but it costs nothing to ask before you sign.

faq.q: Can a divorce or criminal defense lawyer work on contingency?
faq.a: No. ABA Model Rule 1.5(d) bars contingency fees for representing a criminal defendant and in divorce matters where the fee depends on securing the divorce or on the amount of alimony, support or property awarded.
